newsitem.title: USA: Clinton said to approve foreign affairs merger.
newsitem.headline: Clinton said to approve foreign affairs merger.

text.p: President Clinton has approved a broad reorganization of foreign affairs operations that would merge two independent agencies with the State Department and aims to appease critics who are blocking administration priorities, officials said on Thursday.

The plan, worked out by Vice President Al Gore, would integrate the U.S. Information Agency (USIA) and the Arms Control and Disarmament Agency into the State Department over the next two years, the officials said.

The independent Agency for International Development, which administers development aid and humanitarian assistance, would also be partly subsumed by the State Department but would still retain considerable autonomy, officials said.

Republican Sen. Jesse Helms of North Carolina, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and other critics, had pressed the administration to effect the merger before they would consider increasing funds for the State Department, which has suffered considerable spending cuts in recent years.
There also were hints Helms would not let the Chemical Weapons Treaty, which his committee oversees, be acted on by the Senate until the administration agreed to the reorganization.
"There's been a deal worked out," a senior U.S. official told Reuters.
The changes would be accompanied by an intensive internal reform programme at the State Department to "make sure we don't have too many overlapping bureaus," he said.
Under the new plan, "by end of 1999 we will have integrated the four agencies creating a more effective and powerful agency" for handling U.S. diplomacy, he added.

U.S. officials said the Arms Control and Disarmament Agency (ACDA), established as an independent voice for arms control during the Cold War, would be fully integrated into the State Department within one year.
USIA, which had a Cold War mission to promulgate official U.S. views to the world, would be merged in two years.
